plain_language: The general election is held on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November.
detail: Federal, state, legislative, county, township and school board offices are decided in even-numbered years. Presidential electors vote in the same election every four years (IC 3-10-2-3 points to 3 U.S.C. 1). 2026: Nov 3.

plain_language: The primary election is held on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in May in years with a general election.
detail: Examples: May 7, 2024; May 5, 2026. Municipal primaries are on a separate schedule (see municipal_cycle). The 2020 primary was moved to June 2, 2020 by executive order.

plain_language: City and town offices, including mayors, are elected in odd-numbered years, every four years.
detail: Municipal primaries are in May 2023, 2027, 2031 and every four years after, with the general election in November. Mayoral elections were held in 2023 and are next in 2027 (state forms list city or town office elections for 2027).

plain_language: For the 2027 municipal primary (May 4, 2027), candidates for city office and for town office in towns of 3,500 or more may file a declaration of candidacy from January 6 to noon February 5, 2027. Independent and minor-party candidates may file a petition of nomination from January 6 to noon June 30, 2027. The municipal election is November 2, 2027.
detail: The Election Division's 2027 calendar brochure (law as of August 2026) prints January 6, 2027 as the first day for Democratic and Republican declarations and for independent or minor-party petitions, noon February 5 for declarations, noon June 30 for petitions to reach the county voter registration office and noon July 15 for the consent and certified petition. The 2026 calendar names the forms (CAN-42 with CAN-12; CAN-44, CAN-45 for petitions). The dates match IC 3-8-2-4 (118 and 88 days before the primary) and IC 3-8-6-10.

plain_language: In even-numbered years voters choose federal, state and legislative offices plus county, township and school board offices.
detail: Cycles differ by office: the Governor and Attorney General are on the ballot in presidential years (2024, 2028); the Secretary of State, Treasurer and Comptroller in midterm years (2022, 2026). County row offices are split between 2022 and 2026 and 2020 and 2024 groups.

plain_language: The registration deadline is 29 days before an election.
detail: For the 2026 general election: Oct 5, 2026. For the 2026 primary: April 6, 2026. Eligibility: U.S. citizen, Indiana resident, at least 18 by the next general or municipal election, not in prison after a conviction, and living in the precinct 30 days before the election.

plain_language: Indiana holds party primaries but does not register voters by party; each voter picks one party's ballot at the polls.
detail: The ballot choice is recorded in the public record. Ballotpedia calls the system closed by law while officials describe it as semi-open. A poll worker may challenge a voter who did not vote that party's candidates in the last general election and does not intend to in the coming one. To run in a party's primary, a candidate's two most recent Indiana primary votes must have been in that party's primary, or the party's county chair must certify the candidate as a member; a nonpartisan ballot in either of those primaries also needs the chair's certification (IC 3-8-2-7(a)(4)). Bills in 2025 to tighten the system did not pass the Senate.

plain_language: Major-party nominees for Secretary of State, Treasurer and Comptroller are chosen at party conventions, not primaries.
detail: Per Wikipedia coverage of the 2026 races; the statute was not read.

plain_language: Primary candidates file a Declaration of Candidacy; precinct committeeperson candidates file a separate form.
detail: Forms: CAN-2 (Declaration of Candidacy for Primary Nomination in 2026) and CAN-37 (precinct committee or delegate). The 2027 city and town primary uses CAN-42 (Declaration of Candidacy for Municipal Primary Nomination in 2027) with CAN-12 (Statement of Economic Interests).

plain_language: Independent and minor-party candidates reach the November ballot by petition instead of a primary.
detail: Petition of Nomination forms for 2026: CAN-19 (federal, state, legislative and judicial) and CAN-21 (other local offices), with the consent form CAN-20. School board candidates use CAN-34 on a separate window (May 19 to noon June 18 in 2026; see school_board_filing). By statute a petition may be filed from the first day a primary declaration of candidacy may be filed in the election year until noon June 30 before the election; the county voter registration office certifies and files it by noon July 15 (IC 3-8-6-10). For 2026, petitions were due by noon June 30 and the consent form (CAN-20) by noon July 15. For 2027 city and town offices (CAN-44) the Election Division's 2027 calendar prints January 6 through noon June 30, 2027 at the county voter registration office, and noon July 15 for the consent and certified petition.

plain_language: The number of valid signatures needed depends on the office.
detail: Rule: a petition of nomination must be signed by voters equal to 2% of the total vote cast at the last election for Secretary of State in the election district the candidate seeks to represent (fractions disregarded); if the district lies inside one precinct and is not the whole precinct, at least 5 voters (IC 3-8-6-3). Example: for the 2026 Secretary of State race an independent needed 36,943 valid signatures, reported by the Capital Chronicle.

plain_language: A candidate for a local office or school board office must be registered to vote in the election district the candidate seeks to represent by the filing deadline.
detail: Judges of city and town courts are exempt from this requirement.

plain_language: Residency before the election: county offices one year in the county (commissioners and council members also six months in their district); mayor, council member and clerk of a second or third class city one year in the city (council members six months in their district); school board one year in the school corporation (and one year in the election district if the seat is for part of it); town council members must live in their district, if the town has districts.
detail: IC 3-8-1-20 (auditor, recorder, treasurer, sheriff, coroner, surveyor), -21 (commissioner), -22 (county council), -26 (mayor), -27 (common council), -28 (city clerk), -29 (town council), -34 (school board). None of these sections states a minimum age. Township trustee residency is in IC 36-6-4-2.

plain_language: Local and school board candidates file campaign finance reports with the county election board. Pre-election reports are dated 25 days before the nomination date and 25 days before the general or municipal election and are due at noon 7 days later; an annual report covering the year to December 31 is due at noon on the third Wednesday in January.
detail: Reports use form CFA-4; a supplemental large-contribution report (CFA-11) is due within 48 hours for large contributions received shortly before an election (Election Division calendar). 2026 examples: pre-primary report due noon April 17, 2026; annual report due noon January 20, 2027. 2027 dates printed in the Election Division's 2027 calendar: pre-primary period ends April 9, report due noon April 16, 2027; pre-election period ends October 8, report due noon October 15, 2027; annual report for 2027 due noon January 19, 2028. In municipal years city and town candidates file the pre-primary and pre-election reports even when no primary or election is held for their office (IC 3-9-5-9(d)).

plain_language: Indiana has straight-party voting: a voter can mark a party once to vote for all of that party's candidates, but it does not count for at-large offices where more than one person is elected or for school board.
detail: A voter can still mark individual candidates. For offices where more than one candidate is elected at large, and for school board offices, a separate mark for each candidate is needed. In 2026 the St. Joseph County results show 49,335 straight-ticket ballots. Indiana did not eliminate straight-ticket voting in 2019.

plain_language: From 2027, a straight-party vote will also count for at-large offices where several people are elected, unless the voter marks individual candidates for that office.
detail: HEA 1377 (P.L. 99-2026). Covers county council at-large, township board, city council at-large and town council at-large seats. If the voter marks any individual candidate in such a race, the straight-party vote does not apply to that race and only the individual marks count. Does not apply to school board elections. At-large offices will be placed on the ballot with the other offices of the same unit of government.

plain_language: Straight-party voting did not apply to at-large multi-seat offices before 2027.
detail: IC 3-11-2-10's amendment history lists P.L.21-2016 (reported as Senate Enrolled Act 61 of 2016), and Ballot Access News (March 31, 2016) reports that Gov. Pence signed SB 61 on March 21, 2016 and that the law kept the straight-ticket device but required voters who use it to vote separately for local partisan offices with more than one seat. The pre-2016 text and the act's effective date were not read.

plain_language: In-person early voting starts 28 days before the election and ends at noon the day before Election Day.
detail: By statute the absentee voter board in the circuit court clerk's office must offer at least 7 hours on each of the two Saturdays before Election Day; the county election board may also authorize at least 4 hours on the third Saturday. Counties under 20,000 people may, with election-board approval, reduce the two Saturdays to a minimum of 4 hours each.

plain_language: In a county that has adopted vote centers, a registered voter of the county may vote at any vote center in the county on Election Day, regardless of the voter's precinct.
detail: The county election board adopts a vote-center plan only by unanimous vote of the whole board, after two public hearings at least 30 days apart, with resolutions from the county executive and fiscal body; the order and plan are filed with the Election Division. A plan must provide vote centers for primary, general, special and municipal elections, but may leave out towns under 3,500 people in the municipal elections of 2023, 2027, 2031 and every fourth year after.

plain_language: A voter may vote by mail only for a reason listed in state law.
detail: The statute lists reasons including: expecting to be away from the county for the full 12 hours the polls are open, working as an election official or watcher, illness or injury, having a disability, being an elderly voter, caring for someone confined at home, being scheduled to work for the full polling period, military or overseas service, religious observance, participating in the address confidentiality program, being a deployed National Guard member or public safety officer, being a serious sex offender as defined by law, and lacking transportation to the polls. The research listed 11 reasons; the statute page lists more.

plain_language: A mail ballot application must be received by 11:59 pm 12 days before the election, and the voted ballot must arrive by 6 pm on Election Day.
detail: Postmarks do not count. Deadline timing comes from the Secretary of State page; IC 3-11-4-3 sets the application time.

plain_language: Since July 1, 2023 a mail ballot application must include a copy of a photo ID or an ID number.
detail: Accepted numbers: driver's license or state ID number, voter ID number or the last four digits of the Social Security number.

plain_language: A voter must show proof of identification to vote in person.
detail: A voter who cannot or will not show ID, or whose ID does not meet the legal standard, may be challenged and votes a provisional ballot after signing an affidavit. Voters casting an in-person ballot at a polling site in a state-licensed care facility where they live do not need to show ID.

plain_language: Elections in Indiana may not be decided by ranked choice voting.
Since 2025 school board candidates may list a party, list independent, or list no party, and there is no primary for the seats.
detail: SEA 287 (2025): signed by Gov. Braun May 6, 2025; effective July 1, 2025; first used in November 2026. The Senate passed it 26-24 and the House removed a primary requirement. To list the Democratic or Republican Party, a candidate's two most recent Indiana primary votes must have been in that party's primary, or the party's county chair must certify the candidate; a minor-party, independent or no-party choice cannot be challenged on party grounds (IC 3-8-2.5-2.5; IC 3-8-2.5-7). About half of the 1,034 candidates statewide listed no party in 2026 (Chalkbeat, July 2026).

plain_language: School board candidates are grouped on the ballot by party and listed in order of that party's finish in the county in the last Secretary of State race.
detail: SEA 25, P.L. 7-2026. Candidates who list no party appear after the party groups. Names within a group are alphabetical. From 2027 a ballot's voting instructions for vote-for-more-than-one school board seats change.

plain_language: School board candidates file a petition of nomination (CAN-34) with the county election board of the county holding most of the school corporation's population, from the day voter registration reopens after the primary until noon 30 days later; for 2026 that was May 19 to noon June 18. The petition needs 10 registered-voter signatures (from the board member district in a metropolitan school corporation; from the school corporation in a community school corporation).
detail: Each candidate also files a Statement of Economic Interests (CAN-12). The form notes that some school corporations have additional petition requirements; the 2026 Candidate Guide names South Bend (IC 20-23-15) and Mishawaka (IC 20-23-17) among the boards organized by their own statutes. Which other St. Joseph County corporations are metropolitan or community was not determined.

plain_language: A vacancy in the General Assembly is filled by a caucus of the departing member's party precinct committeepersons from that district.
detail: The caucus meets within 30 days of the vacancy; the state party chair sets the time and place and gives at least 10 days' notice; a majority vote selects the successor; the Secretary of State certifies the pick.

plain_language: Many vacancies in local offices and some school board seats are filled by a caucus of the departing official's party.
detail: The county chair of the party gives notice within 10 days; the party's precinct committeepersons from every precinct whose voters could vote for the departing official at the last election for the office take part (appointed committeepersons must have held the post 30 days before the vacancy); the caucus chooses by majority vote, by secret ballot when more than one person seeks the seat (IC 3-13-11-3, -5, -10). The person chosen serves pro tempore under Art. 2 sec. 11 of the constitution. Which offices use a caucus depends on the statute for each office.

plain_language: Precinct committeepersons are elected in the primary and take part in party caucuses; county party chairs are elected by the committeepersons.
detail: By statute precinct committeemen are elected in the primary every four years, on a different cycle for each major party: Republican Party committeemen in May 2024, 2028, 2032 and every four years after (IC 3-10-1-4.6), and other committeemen, including the Democratic Party's, in May 2026, 2030, 2034 and every four years after (IC 3-10-1-4.5). The 2026 Candidate Guide confirms Democratic committeemen on the 2026 primary ballot and Republican committeemen in 2028. Next elections: Republican May 2028, Democratic May 2030. How a county chair is chosen is set by each party's rules; no statute was found and the party rules were not read, so that part stays low confidence.

plain_language: The Governor serves a four-year term and cannot serve more than eight years in any twelve-year period.
The county clerk, auditor, recorder, treasurer, sheriff and coroner may serve no more than 8 years in any 12-year period.
detail: Commissioners, council members, assessors, surveyors and prosecutors are not on the list. Service by a person chosen to fill a vacancy pro tempore does not count. Read through a search summary and a state brochure, not the constitution text.

plain_language: Four counties (Lake, St. Joseph, Allen and Marion) choose superior court judges by merit selection instead of partisan election.
detail: A nominating commission screens applicants and sends the Governor a short list; the Governor appoints. Details vary by county statute. Marion County has used merit selection since 2017. A 2021 law (HEA 1453) changed the Lake and St. Joseph commissions.

plain_language: A merit-selected superior court judge faces a yes-or-no retention vote at the general election before the term ends.
detail: The ballot asks whether the judge shall be retained for an additional term. A judge who wants to stay files a statement with the Secretary of State by noon July 15 of the election year. If a majority votes No, the office becomes vacant on January 1 and the Governor fills it. (St. Joseph County statute text; other merit counties have their own sections.)

plain_language: Ballot lines marked 'Retain Justice' in county results are statewide appellate retention questions and may involve Court of Appeals judges, not only Supreme Court justices.
detail: Check each name against the Indiana Judicial Branch roster before describing a seat.

plain_language: Indiana has no statewide citizen initiative or referendum, and no citizen recall of officials.
detail: The legislature can send constitutional amendments to voters. Ballotpedia says there is no citizen-initiated ballot measure process at the local level either, and that Indiana is one of two states without one.

plain_language: A school corporation or other local unit can ask voters to approve extra property tax in a referendum.
detail: Operating referendums fund school operations; other referendums approve controlled projects. The Department of Local Government Finance publishes referendum information. Mechanics were not collected.

plain_language: A regular session in an odd-numbered year must end by April 29; in an even-numbered year it must end by March 14.
detail: The April 29 date for odd-year sessions beginning after 2022 is on the FindLaw statute page. March 14 for the short session comes from search summaries of the same statute, not the page fetched. The legislative-day limits (61 and 30) were not checked.

plain_language: The General Assembly meets in November after the election to organize, then reconvenes in January.
detail: The first regular session convenes on the third Tuesday after the first Monday of November in even-numbered years to organize, elect officers and take the oath, then adjourns to a date set by resolution and must reconvene no later than the fourth Monday in January.

plain_language: The House has 100 members serving two-year terms; the Senate has 50 members serving four-year terms with staggered elections. There are no term limits.
Two-thirds of each chamber must be present to do business: 67 House members and 34 senators.
detail: The same two-thirds figure is the supermajority number referred to in news coverage of the 2026 election. A smaller group may meet, postpone proceedings from day to day and require absent members to attend.

plain_language: The Governor's veto can be overridden by a majority of all members elected to each chamber (51 in the House, 26 in the Senate).
detail: Most states require two-thirds. Seen through secondary text of the constitution (amended 1972 and 1990); the official in.gov text was not retrieved.
